rationale: Haiku applied a blanket heuristic ('basics in title = concrete') that mischaracterizes most of these topics. The actual content reveals that 5 of the 8 topics require reasoning about invisible mechanisms, generalized principles, or abstract relationships -- hallmarks of abstract-reasoning. However, 3 topics are genuinely better placed at concrete-operations. (1) ACCEPT boiling-and-simmering: This is observational and procedural -- watch for bubble size, adjust heat. The 'boiling point' explanation is supplementary; the skill is learned by looking at a pot. Prerequisites are just kitchen safety and reading recipes. Concrete. (2) ACCEPT baking-basics: The topic's own prerequisites include fractions and measurement, but the TOPIC ITSELF is about following procedures with physical ingredients -- measuring flour, mixing batter, setting oven temperature. It's the concrete foundation that later topics (bread-baking, pastry) build abstract understanding upon. (3) ACCEPT breading-coating-techniques: Three-step procedural sequence (flour, egg, breadcrumbs) learned entirely through hands-on practice. Understanding WHY each layer works is enrichment, not the core skill. (4) REJECT basic-flavor-components-salt-acid-fat: This is explicitly about understanding abstract flavor PRINCIPLES -- why salt enhances perception, how acid balances richness, how fat carries flavor. These are invisible mechanisms generalized across all cooking. Not concrete. (5) REJECT basic-nutrition-fundamentals: Calories, macronutrients, metabolic functions -- these are abstract categories requiring reasoning about invisible processes. You cannot see a calorie or directly observe protein synthesis. (6) REJECT braising-and-slow-cooking: Understanding collagen-to-gelatin conversion at specific temperatures, why time transforms tough cuts -- this is reasoning about molecular chemistry applied to cooking. The technique requires understanding WHY, not just following steps. (7) REJECT bread-baking-yeast-fermentation: Yeast metabolism, CO2 production, gluten protein networks, fermentation chemistry -- this is applied biochemistry. The topic explicitly discusses glutenin and gliadin hydration. Firmly abstract-reasoning. (8) REJECT cooking-conversions-scaling: This topic requires proportional reasoning, unit conversion across measurement systems, and understanding NON-LINEAR scaling (leavening agents don't scale proportionally). It has hard prerequisites on unit-rates and metric conversions. This is applied mathematics at the abstract-reasoning level.
